options.a: Antibodies in the plasma with known reagent red cells
options.b: Antigens on the red cells with known antibodies
options.c: Antibodies already bound to the red cells with AHG reagent
options.d: Fetal red cells in maternal blood by acid elution staining

distractorExplanations.a: That describes reverse typing, which uses known A1 and B cells to detect antibodies in the patient's plasma.
distractorExplanations.c: Detecting antibody coating the patient's red cells with AHG is the direct antiglobulin test, not forward typing.
distractorExplanations.d: Acid elution (Kleihauer-Betke) quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage; forward typing detects ABO antigens on red cells.

options.a: Patient red cells plus anti-A and anti-B reagents
options.b: Patient plasma plus group O screening cells
options.c: Patient serum/plasma plus A1 and B cells
options.d: Patient serum plus A2 and O cells at AHG phase

distractorExplanations.a: Testing patient red cells with anti-A and anti-B is forward typing; reverse typing tests the patient's plasma.
distractorExplanations.b: O screening cells are used for the antibody screen, which detects unexpected non-ABO antibodies.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverse typing uses A1 and B cells read at immediate spin; A2 cells and the AHG phase belong to other workups.

options.a: 4+ with A1 cells, negative with B cells
options.b: Negative with both A1 and B cells
options.c: 4+ with both A1 and B cells
options.d: 4+ with B cells, negative with A1 cells

distractorExplanations.a: That is the reverse pattern of a group B person, whose plasma contains anti-A that agglutinates A1 cells.
distractorExplanations.b: No reaction with A1 or B cells is the group AB reverse pattern, since AB plasma lacks both anti-A and anti-B.
distractorExplanations.c: Reactions with both A1 and B cells is the group O reverse pattern, because group O plasma has anti-A and anti-B.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-004.explanation: Landsteiner. This item asks: “A type A patient should reverse as:”. The matching answer is: 4+ with B cells, negative with A1 cells (typical). Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. This is the typical pattern; weak or missing reactions need a discrepancy workup.

options.a: It detects IgG that does not agglutinate in saline
options.b: It detects IgM that agglutinates at room temperature
options.c: It lowers the zeta potential so red cells come closer
options.d: It removes bound antibody from red cells for identification

distractorExplanations.b: IgM antibodies agglutinate directly at immediate spin or room temperature; AHG is needed to detect IgG coating.
distractorExplanations.c: Reducing zeta potential is the job of enhancement media such as LISS or PEG, not the antiglobulin reagent.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing bound antibody from red cells is an elution; AHG bridges IgG-coated cells to make agglutination visible.

options.a: Expected anti-A and anti-B in the patient's plasma
options.b: Unexpected red-cell antibodies in the patient
options.c: Antibody already coating the patient's red cells
options.d: Unexpected antigens on the donor unit's red cells

distractorExplanations.a: Detecting expected anti-A and anti-B is the reverse ABO type; the screen looks for unexpected non-ABO antibodies.
distractorExplanations.c: Antibody bound in vivo to the patient's red cells is detected by the DAT; the screen tests plasma for free antibody.
distractorExplanations.d: The screen tests patient plasma for antibodies, not donor cells for antigens; antigen typing is a separate test.

options.a: Maternal IgM anti-A crossing the placenta
options.b: Physiologic jaundice from immature liver conjugation
options.c: Maternal IgG on baby cells — HDFN workup
options.d: Hereditary spherocytosis inherited from a parent

distractorExplanations.a: IgM does not cross the placenta; HDFN results from maternal IgG antibodies coating the baby's red cells.
distractorExplanations.b: Physiologic jaundice is a liver conjugation issue with a negative DAT; a positive DAT shows antibody coating.
distractorExplanations.d: Hereditary spherocytosis causes neonatal hemolysis with a negative DAT; a positive DAT points to maternal antibody.

options.a: A D-positive mother delivers a D-negative baby
options.b: An Rh-negative mother already has anti-D from a prior pregnancy
options.c: An Rh-positive patient receives Rh-negative red cells
options.d: An Rh-negative mother is at risk of forming anti-D

distractorExplanations.a: A D-positive mother cannot form anti-D, so RhIG is not indicated whatever the baby's type.
distractorExplanations.b: RhIG cannot help once anti-D has actively formed; it prevents sensitization rather than treating it.
distractorExplanations.c: A D-positive recipient cannot form anti-D; RhIG protects D-negative people exposed to D-positive cells.

options.a: Clerically identical at the bedside
options.b: Issued once the crossmatch passes, without a label check
options.c: Matched by patient name alone at the bedside
options.d: Warmed in an unmonitored water bath before every issue

distractorExplanations.b: A compatible crossmatch does not replace the clerical check of unit, tag, and patient identifiers at issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Name alone is insufficient; two identifiers plus unit number and ABO/Rh must match the tag and record.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine warming is not required, and blood warmers must be cleared, monitored devices, not open water baths.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-009.explanation: Clerical error kills. This item asks: “A unit for transfusion must be:”. The matching answer is: Clerically identical at the bedside — the MLT's issue check is not optional. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. The MLT's issue check is not optional.

options.a: At 1–6 °C, like red blood cells
options.b: Frozen, then thawed per procedure
options.c: At 20–24 °C with gentle agitation
options.d: Frozen at −18 °C, then refrozen if unused

distractorExplanations.a: 1–6 °C is red cell storage; FFP is stored frozen at −18 °C or colder and refrigerated only after thawing.
distractorExplanations.c: Room temperature with agitation is platelet storage; FFP stays frozen until it is thawed for use.
distractorExplanations.d: Thawed plasma cannot be refrozen; once thawed it is kept at 1–6 °C and relabeled with its new dating.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-010.explanation: Product, temperature, time. This item asks: “FFP is stored:”. The matching answer is: Frozen, then thawed per procedure — not as a fridge RBC. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. It is not stored refrigerated like red cells until after thawing.

options.a: Issue the unit if the antibody screen was negative
options.b: Issue the unit with a slower infusion rate
options.c: Do not issue that unit — investigate
options.d: Repeat at immediate spin and issue if negative

distractorExplanations.a: An incompatible AHG crossmatch overrides a negative screen; it may reveal an antibody to a low-incidence antigen.
distractorExplanations.b: Slowing the infusion does not make an incompatible unit safe; it can still cause a hemolytic reaction.
distractorExplanations.d: An immediate-spin crossmatch misses IgG antibodies, so a negative IS result does not cancel AHG incompatibility.

options.a: Frozen at −18 °C or colder, like FFP
options.b: At 1–6 °C without agitation, like RBCs
options.c: At room temp without agitation for 30 days
options.d: With agitation at room temp for their dating

distractorExplanations.a: Platelets are not frozen in routine practice; freezing is the storage condition for FFP and cryoprecipitate.
distractorExplanations.b: Refrigeration at 1–6 °C is red cell storage; routine platelets are kept at 20–24 °C with continuous agitation.
distractorExplanations.c: Without agitation platelets lose gas exchange, and room-temperature dating is about 5–7 days, not 30 days.

options.a: A physician-released emergency — still document
options.b: A routine release once the type is known
options.c: An MLT decision made without a physician order
options.d: Exempt from documentation until testing is done

distractorExplanations.b: Uncrossmatched release is an emergency exception, not routine; it needs a physician's signed request.
distractorExplanations.c: The MLT cannot authorize uncrossmatched blood; the ordering physician signs for the risk of emergency release.
distractorExplanations.d: Emergency release still requires documentation, the signed request, and completion of compatibility testing afterward.

options.a: Repeat crossmatch on the original sample before any clerical check
options.b: Clerical check and a DAT / visual hemolysis per SOP — stop the unit
options.c: Slowing the transfusion and giving an antipyretic, then resuming the unit
options.d: Antibody identification panel on the donor unit's plasma first

distractorExplanations.a: The clerical check comes first because misidentification is the most common cause; repeating the old crossmatch can miss it.
distractorExplanations.c: Fever can signal acute hemolysis; the transfusion is stopped, not slowed and resumed, until the workup is done.
distractorExplanations.d: A panel on donor plasma is not the first step; the post-transfusion sample gets a clerical check, hemolysis check, and DAT.

options.a: An official ASCP MLT practice form released by the Board of Certification
options.b: MLS-level practice that mirrors the generalist scientist exam form
options.c: Independent technician-level lab practice — not the MLS exam form
options.d: A state licensure exam for clinical laboratory personnel

distractorExplanations.a: UniPrep is an independent diagnostic; the ASCP Board of Certification does not release its exam forms for this mock.
distractorExplanations.b: MLS is the scientist-level exam; this mock targets the technician-level MLT scope instead.
distractorExplanations.d: State licensure (for example California or New York) is separate from ASCP certification and from this independent mock.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-015.explanation: Same benches, technician items. This item asks: “This MLT mock is:”. The matching answer is: Independent technician-level lab practice — not the MLS exam form and not ASCP's test. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. It is not ASCP's test.

options.a: Sodium and chloride from dilution
options.b: Glucose and albumin from cell release
options.c: Haptoglobin from free hemoglobin binding
options.d: Potassium and LD among others

distractorExplanations.a: Hemolysis releases intracellular contents; sodium and chloride are higher in plasma and are minimally affected.
distractorExplanations.b: Red cells do not release glucose or albumin; hemolysis raises analytes concentrated inside cells such as K, LD and AST.
distractorExplanations.c: Haptoglobin falls in in-vivo hemolysis as it binds free hemoglobin; in-vitro hemolysis does not raise it.

options.a: Skeletal muscle injury such as rhabdomyolysis
options.b: Myocardial injury workup — timing matters
options.c: Heart failure staging by ventricular stretch
options.d: Liver injury workup alongside ALT and AST

distractorExplanations.a: Skeletal muscle injury is assessed with CK and myoglobin; cardiac troponin I and T are specific to heart muscle.
distractorExplanations.c: Ventricular stretch is measured by BNP or NT-proBNP, not troponin, which reflects myocyte injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Troponin is cardiac-specific; liver injury is assessed with ALT, AST and synthetic markers, not troponin.

options.a: Falsely high from photo-oxidation
options.b: Unchanged if tested within 24 hours
options.c: Falsely low — protect from light
options.d: Falsely low only if the tube is refrigerated

distractorExplanations.a: Light breaks bilirubin down by photo-oxidation, which lowers rather than raises the measured value.
distractorExplanations.b: Light degrades bilirubin within about an hour; prompt testing does not rescue a tube left exposed.
distractorExplanations.d: Refrigeration slows degradation; the error comes from light exposure, not from storage temperature.

options.a: BUN and the urine creatinine concentration
options.b: Serum creatinine, age, sex, and race
options.c: Serum albumin and the urine protein ratio
options.d: Creatinine (and age/sex as the equation uses)

distractorExplanations.a: Urine creatinine is used in a measured creatinine clearance; eGFR equations use serum creatinine with age and sex.
distractorExplanations.b: The current CKD-EPI 2021 equation removed the race coefficient; it uses creatinine, age, and sex.
distractorExplanations.c: Albumin and urine protein assess kidney damage (albuminuria), not an estimate of filtration rate.

options.a: Interfere with spectrophotometric assays
options.b: Falsely raise potassium by releasing it from cells
options.c: Be cleared by saline dilution for every analyte
options.d: Falsely lower bilirubin by light degradation

distractorExplanations.b: Releasing potassium from cells is hemolysis interference; lipemia acts through light scatter and volume displacement.
distractorExplanations.c: Dilution can lower lipemia but distorts some results; ultracentrifugation is the usual clearing step.
distractorExplanations.d: Light degradation lowers bilirubin in exposed tubes; lipemia interferes through turbidity, not photo-oxidation.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-chemistry-021.explanation: Lipemia is preanalytical. This item asks: “A lipemic sample can:”. The matching answer is: Interfere with spectrophotometric assays — ultracentrifuge or comment per SOP. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Ultracentrifuge or add a comment per SOP.

options.a: The last 2–3 days of glucose
options.b: Weeks of glucose exposure
options.c: Glycated albumin as a fructosamine level
options.d: Fasting glucose on the draw day

distractorExplanations.a: HbA1c integrates glycemia over the red cell lifespan, about 2–3 months, not the last few days.
distractorExplanations.c: Fructosamine measures glycated serum proteins, mainly albumin, over 2–3 weeks; HbA1c is glycated hemoglobin.
distractorExplanations.d: A fasting glucose is a single-point value; HbA1c reflects average exposure over weeks to months.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-chemistry-022.explanation: Glycation window. This item asks: “HbA1c reflects:”. The matching answer is: Weeks of glucose exposure, not this morning's donut alone. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Clinically it reflects about 2–3 months of average glucose.

options.a: (Cl + HCO3) − Na as measured
options.b: Na − Cl, ignoring bicarbonate
options.c: Na − (Cl + HCO3) as your lab calculates
options.d: Measured minus calculated osmolality

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the subtraction; the gap is sodium minus the measured anions, which gives a positive value.
distractorExplanations.b: Omitting bicarbonate gives a different value; the standard anion gap subtracts both chloride and bicarbonate.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the osmolal gap, used for unmeasured osmoles such as toxic alcohols, not the anion gap.

options.a: Report the result with a hemolysis comment
options.b: Dilute the sample with saline and rerun
options.c: Report if the result is within reference range
options.d: Do not report — recast or recollect

distractorExplanations.a: A clot flag concerns sampling, not hemolysis; results from a clot-flagged aspiration are not reportable.
distractorExplanations.b: Dilution does not remove a fibrin clot; the specimen must be inspected, respun, or recollected.
distractorExplanations.c: A short sample from a clot can give normal-looking but false values; reference-range results are not exempt.

options.a: Kept at room temperature to prevent hemolysis
options.b: On ice and assayed fast
options.c: Collected in a serum tube and allowed to clot
options.d: Refrigerated overnight and run in batch

distractorExplanations.a: Room temperature lets red cell metabolism and deamination raise ammonia, so samples go on ice.
distractorExplanations.c: Clotting time lets ammonia rise; ammonia uses EDTA or heparin plasma placed on ice and separated quickly.
distractorExplanations.d: Delay raises ammonia even when refrigerated; it is analyzed within about 30 minutes or separated and frozen.

options.a: Expected daily variation to be released as is
options.b: Instrument drift that QC will correct later
options.c: Wrong patient or IV fluid mix-up — investigate
options.d: A dilution error to fix by applying a factor

distractorExplanations.a: A large overnight jump exceeds expected biological variation; delta failures are investigated before release.
distractorExplanations.b: Drift is caught by QC before patient release; a single-patient delta failure points to identity or collection.
distractorExplanations.d: Applying a factor without investigation can hide a wrong-patient sample; the cause must be found first.

options.a: A random draw with the dose time added later
options.b: A trough drawn just after the dose ends
options.c: A serum gel-separator tube for every drug
options.d: The draw time relative to the dose

distractorExplanations.a: Peak and trough interpretation needs exact draw and dose times documented at collection, not reconstructed.
distractorExplanations.b: A trough is drawn just before the next dose; just after the dose is the peak window.
distractorExplanations.c: Gel separators can absorb some drugs, so many therapeutic drug assays require plain red-top tubes.

options.a: Repeated and correlated — do not treat a strip error
options.b: Treated immediately, as POC meters are calibrated
options.c: Reported with a comment and not repeated
options.d: Confirmed on a capillary sample from the same finger

distractorExplanations.b: Calibration does not prevent strip, hematocrit, or sampling errors; a discordant result is repeated and correlated.
distractorExplanations.c: A comment does not resolve a discordant value; it is repeated and confirmed with a laboratory method.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeating from the same site can repeat the error; confirmation uses a venous laboratory glucose.

options.a: The unit clerk, who passes it to the nurse
options.b: The licensed caregiver on the list — read back
options.c: A voicemail for the ordering physician
options.d: The licensed caregiver, without read-back

distractorExplanations.a: Critical values go directly to a licensed caregiver who can act, not through clerical staff.
distractorExplanations.c: Voicemail is not acceptable for criticals; the result must reach a person with documented read-back.
distractorExplanations.d: Read-back verification is required to confirm that the critical value was heard and recorded correctly.

options.a: Released if the WBC count is within range
options.b: Rerun on the analyzer until the flag clears
options.c: A smear review — do not auto-release if SOP says hold
options.d: Resolved by a manual WBC count on a hemocytometer

distractorExplanations.a: Blasts can occur with a normal WBC count; a blast flag triggers smear review whatever the count.
distractorExplanations.b: Rerunning does not verify morphology; the flag requires a smear review rather than repeat counts.
distractorExplanations.d: A manual count verifies the number of cells, not their identity; blasts need smear morphology review.

options.a: Iron deficiency or thalassemia trait
options.b: Anemia of chronic disease or acute blood loss
options.c: Sideroblastic anemia from lead poisoning
options.d: A macrocytic picture (B12/folate/liver/marrow)

distractorExplanations.a: Iron deficiency and thalassemia trait produce a low MCV (microcytic), not a high MCV.
distractorExplanations.b: Chronic disease and acute blood loss usually give normocytic indices, not a raised MCV.
distractorExplanations.c: Lead poisoning and sideroblastic anemia typically give microcytic or dimorphic indices, not macrocytosis.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-hematology-032.explanation: Use the indices. This item asks: “MCV high with anemia suggests:”. The matching answer is: A macrocytic picture (B12/folate/liver/marrow) — not a micro iron story. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. It does not point to microcytic iron deficiency.

options.a: Falsely lower the count — citrate recollect as SOP
options.b: Falsely raise the platelet count from large clumps
options.c: Falsely lower the count — heparin recollect as SOP
options.d: Lower the hemoglobin by trapping red cells

distractorExplanations.b: Clumps are not counted as many single platelets; they lower the platelet count instead of raising it.
distractorExplanations.c: Heparin tubes promote platelet clumping too; sodium citrate is the usual recollection tube for EDTA clumping.
distractorExplanations.d: Platelet clumps do not affect hemoglobin; they may falsely raise the WBC count when counted as leukocytes.

options.a: A specific marker of bacterial infection
options.b: A nonspecific inflammation marker, not a diagnosis
options.c: A test that falls with inflammation and anemia
options.d: A diagnostic test for multiple myeloma alone

distractorExplanations.a: ESR rises in many conditions; procalcitonin is closer to a bacterial-specific marker.
distractorExplanations.c: ESR rises, not falls, with inflammation and anemia because rouleaux form faster.
distractorExplanations.d: Myeloma can raise ESR, but ESR is nonspecific; myeloma is diagnosed with SPEP, immunofixation and marrow.

options.a: Thin film only, once
options.b: Thick and thin, once
options.c: Thick and thin, timed
options.d: Buffy coat stain, once

distractorExplanations.a: Thin films alone miss low parasitemia; thick films for detection plus serial collections are needed.
distractorExplanations.b: A single negative set does not exclude malaria; smears are repeated every 12–24 hours for three sets.
distractorExplanations.d: A buffy coat preparation is not the standard method; thick and thin Giemsa films repeated over time are.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-hematology-035.explanation: Look at the film. This item asks: “A malaria smear is:”. The matching answer is: Thick and thin, timed — not a casual Wright glance as 'negative' without looking. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. A casual Wright-stain glance does not make a smear negative.

options.a: Monitor unfractionated heparin therapy
options.b: Screen for von Willebrand disease
options.c: Monitor low-molecular-weight heparin
options.d: Monitor warfarin-style anticoagulation

distractorExplanations.a: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with the aPTT or anti-Xa level, not the INR.
distractorExplanations.b: von Willebrand disease is evaluated with VWF antigen, activity and factor VIII; the INR is usually normal.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-molecular-weight heparin is monitored, when needed, with anti-Xa levels, not the INR.

options.a: Whether the anemia is microcytic or macrocytic
options.b: Whether the marrow is answering an anemia
options.c: Whether iron stores are depleted
options.d: Whether hemolysis is immune-mediated

distractorExplanations.a: Cell size classification comes from the MCV; the reticulocyte count measures marrow output.
distractorExplanations.c: Iron stores are measured by ferritin; reticulocytes reflect red cell production, not iron reserve.
distractorExplanations.d: Immune-mediated hemolysis is identified by the DAT; reticulocytes rise in many hemolytic causes alike.

options.a: A repeat CBC in one week
options.b: An allergy panel and IgE alone
options.c: A path review / parasite thought
options.d: A bacterial culture workup

distractorExplanations.a: Marked eosinophilia in a traveler suggests parasitic infection; waiting a week delays the needed review.
distractorExplanations.b: Allergy can raise eosinophils, but 40% in a traveler needs pathology review and parasite consideration first.
distractorExplanations.d: Bacterial infection typically causes neutrophilia, not marked eosinophilia; parasites are the key concern.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-hematology-039.explanation: Uncommon diffs get eyes. This item asks: “A differential with 40% eos in a traveler may need:”. The matching answer is: A path review / parasite thought — not auto-file. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. It should not be auto-filed.

options.a: A fibrinogen-degradation marker specific for DIC
options.b: A fibrin-degradation marker that confirms PE when positive
options.c: A clotting factor assay that measures factor XIII
options.d: A fibrin-degradation marker with huge negative-predictive use

distractorExplanations.a: D-dimer comes from cross-linked fibrin, not fibrinogen, and it is not specific for DIC.
distractorExplanations.b: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific; a positive result needs imaging and does not confirm PE.
distractorExplanations.c: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin, but D-dimer is a breakdown product, not a factor activity assay.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-hematology-040.explanation: Pretest probability. This item asks: “D-dimer is:”. The matching answer is: A fibrin-degradation marker with huge negative-predictive use in the right pretest. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Its value depends on the right pretest probability.

options.a: Done as a sterile, timed, labeled procedure
options.b: Done after refrigerating the fluid overnight
options.c: Done on a clotted sample after mixing it well
options.d: Done by automated analyzer on every fluid type

distractorExplanations.b: Cells degrade with delay; body fluid counts are done promptly, not after overnight storage.
distractorExplanations.c: A clotted fluid traps cells and gives an invalid count; EDTA-anticoagulated tubes are used for cell counts.
distractorExplanations.d: Analyzers need validation for each fluid; low counts or some fluids require a manual hemocytometer count.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-hematology-041.explanation: Fluids are STAT-ish. This item asks: “A body-fluid count should be:”. The matching answer is: Done as a sterile, timed, labeled procedure — not a leftover syringe in a pocket. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. A leftover syringe carried in a pocket is not acceptable.

options.a: Distinguish sickle cell disease from sickle trait by reaction strength
options.b: Screen — they do not replace electrophoresis when you need a type
options.c: Detect Hb C and other non-sickling variants
options.d: Confirm HbS reliably in newborns with high HbF

distractorExplanations.a: Solubility is positive in both disease and trait; electrophoresis or HPLC is needed to separate them.
distractorExplanations.c: Solubility tests detect HbS; Hb C and other variants need electrophoresis or HPLC.
distractorExplanations.d: High HbF in newborns can give false negatives, so solubility tests are not used for newborn screening.

options.a: Called at the end of the shift along with the other results
options.b: Reported in the LIS with a critical flag only
options.c: Called — neutropenia is an emergency for the clinician
options.d: Repeated on a new specimen before any call

distractorExplanations.a: Critical values are called promptly; batching them delays treatment of febrile neutropenia.
distractorExplanations.b: An electronic flag does not meet critical-call requirements; a direct call with read-back is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: A plausible critical value is called without waiting for a recollection that delays urgent care.

options.a: Report morphology with a stain-quality comment
options.b: Adjust the microscope light to correct the color
options.c: Too blue means the buffer pH is too acidic
options.d: Fix the stain, do not invent morphology

distractorExplanations.a: Poor staining makes morphology unreliable; the smear is restained rather than reported with a caveat.
distractorExplanations.b: Lighting changes do not fix stain pH or timing errors; buffer pH and staining times must be corrected.
distractorExplanations.c: An overly blue stain usually reflects alkaline buffer or thick films; an acidic buffer makes smears too pink.

options.a: Validating flags and knowing when a smear/path review is required
options.b: Diagnosing leukemia subtypes from the peripheral smear
options.c: Releasing every flagged result promptly to reduce turnaround time
options.d: Recommending treatment based on CBC trends

distractorExplanations.b: Diagnosing leukemia subtypes is the pathologist's role; the MLT flags and refers abnormal findings.
distractorExplanations.c: Flags are resolved, not bypassed; turnaround pressure does not justify releasing unverified results.
distractorExplanations.d: Treatment decisions belong to the clinician; the MLT provides validated results and alerts.

options.a: Acceptable if the port was flushed with saline
options.b: A contaminant risk — redo the draw right
options.c: Acceptable if only the aerobic bottle is filled
options.d: Reliable as long as both sets were drawn from it

distractorExplanations.a: Flushing does not disinfect the hub; lines must be scrubbed, and venipuncture is preferred to reduce contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Skipping the anaerobic bottle does not prevent contamination and reduces recovery of anaerobes.
distractorExplanations.d: Drawing both sets through a dirty port can grow the same contaminant twice, mimicking true bacteremia.

options.a: Streptococci until proven otherwise
options.b: Enterococci from the wound flora
options.c: Staph-like until identified
options.d: Micrococcus as a reportable pathogen

distractorExplanations.a: Streptococci form pairs and chains; clusters suggest staphylococci, confirmed with the catalase test.
distractorExplanations.b: Enterococci appear as pairs and short chains, not grape-like clusters.
distractorExplanations.d: Micrococcus can cluster but is usually a skin contaminant; identification, not assumption, comes first.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-047.explanation: Morphology first. This item asks: “Gram-positive cocci in clusters from a wound are:”. The matching answer is: Staph-like until identified — not a 'strep throat' story. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Do not treat them as a streptococcal finding.

options.a: Formed stool sent to screen for asymptomatic carriage
options.b: Rectal swab after diarrhea resolves
options.c: Stool in formalin for the O&P exam
options.d: Loose stool, not a formed 'just in case'

distractorExplanations.a: Formed stool is rejected because detecting carriage leads to overdiagnosis; unformed stool is tested.
distractorExplanations.b: Testing after resolution or as a test of cure is not recommended because toxin and DNA can persist.
distractorExplanations.c: Formalin preserves parasites but destroys toxin and inhibits NAAT; C. difficile needs unpreserved stool.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-048.explanation: Right specimen. This item asks: “C. difficile testing is on:”. The matching answer is: Loose stool, not a formed 'just in case' as many algorithms say. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Many testing algorithms reject formed stool.

options.a: Mycobacteria suspicions
options.b: Gram-negative rods in urine
options.c: Yeast capsules in CSF
options.d: Spirochetes such as Treponema

distractorExplanations.b: Gram-negative rods are seen on Gram stain; acid-fast stains target organisms with mycolic acid walls.
distractorExplanations.c: The capsule of Cryptococcus is shown with India ink, not with acid-fast staining.
distractorExplanations.d: Spirochetes need darkfield or silver stains; they are not acid-fast organisms.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-049.explanation: AFB has a reason. This item asks: “Acid-fast stain is for:”. The matching answer is: Mycobacteria suspicions — not a routine throat. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. It is not ordered on a routine throat swab.

options.a: Called once the organism is fully identified on culture
options.b: A critical call — do not wait for the full ID to notify
options.c: Reported in the LIS with a routine priority
options.d: Repeated on a second CSF tube before calling

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for identification delays meningitis treatment; the Gram stain finding itself is the critical result.
distractorExplanations.c: Organisms in CSF are a critical result requiring immediate verbal notification, not routine reporting.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeating delays care; the observed organisms are called as found and confirmed on culture later.

options.a: Report results but flag the failed antibiotic
options.b: Report if the patient zones are very large
options.c: Do not report patient AST from that run
options.d: Report results and repeat QC on the next day

distractorExplanations.a: Patient results for the affected drug cannot be reported until the QC failure is corrected.
distractorExplanations.b: Large zones are not exempt; failed QC means the accuracy of that run is unverified.
distractorExplanations.d: Results from a run with failed QC are withheld; deferring QC to the next day releases unverified results.

options.a: A routine stool culture for Salmonella and Shigella
options.b: An ova and parasite exam as the first test
options.c: A stool culture for Campylobacter and E. coli O157
options.d: Not a community Salmonella hunt — think C. diff

distractorExplanations.a: The 3-day rule rejects routine enteric cultures after 3 days of hospitalization; C. difficile testing fits instead.
distractorExplanations.b: O&P has low yield in hospital-onset diarrhea and is also restricted by the 3-day rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Community pathogens such as Campylobacter rarely cause diarrhea that starts after day 3 in hospital.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-052.explanation: Healthcare vs community. This item asks: “A stool culture in a patient hospitalized 5 days with new diarrhea is often:”. The matching answer is: Not a community Salmonella hunt — think C. diff per protocol. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Testing follows the lab's 3-day rule protocol.

options.a: The right swab and media
options.b: A calcium alginate swab
options.c: A dry cotton swab in a tube
options.d: Bacterial transport gel media

distractorExplanations.b: Calcium alginate and wooden swabs can inhibit PCR; flocked synthetic swabs in viral media are used.
distractorExplanations.c: Cotton and dry transport degrade the sample and can inhibit amplification; viral transport media is used.
distractorExplanations.d: Amies or Stuart gel is for bacterial culture; viral PCR uses VTM/UTM or approved molecular media.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-053.explanation: Collection is the test. This item asks: “Viral transport for a PCR must be:”. The matching answer is: The right swab and media — a dry wood swab can kill the test. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. A dry wooden swab can inhibit or ruin the PCR.

options.a: The caregiver once susceptibility results are ready
options.b: The caregiver with organism morphology — read back
options.c: The infection prevention office instead of the nurse
options.d: The caregiver, reporting only positive or negative

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for susceptibilities delays therapy by a day or more; the Gram stain result is called immediately.
distractorExplanations.c: Infection prevention may be notified, but the result must reach the caregiver who can treat the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Morphology such as GPC in clusters guides empiric therapy; a bare 'positive' omits key information.

options.a: Candida in a CSF sample
options.b: Histoplasma in urine antigen
options.c: Cryptococcus in the right host
options.d: Pneumocystis in a BAL sample

distractorExplanations.a: Candida is identified by culture and germ tube; India ink highlights the cryptococcal capsule.
distractorExplanations.b: Histoplasma is detected by its own urine antigen test; CrAg is specific to Cryptococcus.
distractorExplanations.d: Pneumocystis is shown with GMS or DFA staining, not with India ink or cryptococcal antigen.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-055.explanation: Yeast in CSF. This item asks: “India ink / CrAg is in the thought process for:”. The matching answer is: Cryptococcus in the right host — not a strep screen. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. It is not a streptococcal screen.

options.a: A dry swab
options.b: Refrigerated transport
options.c: A sterile cup
options.d: Proper transport

distractorExplanations.a: Dry swabs expose anaerobes to oxygen and drying; tissue or aspirate in anaerobic transport is preferred.
distractorExplanations.b: Refrigeration lets oxygen diffuse in and harms some anaerobes; anaerobic transport is held at room temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: A plain sterile cup admits oxygen; anaerobes need an oxygen-free transport container.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-056.explanation: Oxygen kills anaerobes. This item asks: “Anaerobic culture needs:”. The matching answer is: Proper transport — a dry swab sitting 6 hours is a waste. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. A dry swab sitting for hours is useless for anaerobes.

options.a: A colonization/infection-control tool, not a blood culture
options.b: A diagnostic test for MRSA pneumonia that stands on its own
options.c: A susceptibility test that replaces culture AST
options.d: A screen that detects MRSA bacteremia directly

distractorExplanations.b: Nares PCR has a high negative predictive value for MRSA pneumonia, but a positive result shows colonization.
distractorExplanations.c: PCR detects MRSA markers such as mecA but does not give full susceptibility results for treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Nares swabs sample a colonization site; bloodstream infection is detected by blood culture.

options.a: Full ID and AST on every colony type
options.b: Likely contamination — comment
options.c: A pure culture of the leading organism
options.d: Reported as no growth

distractorExplanations.a: Working up all mixed skin flora wastes resources and produces misleading reports from a poor specimen.
distractorExplanations.c: Subculturing one organism from mixed skin flora implies a pathogen without clinical support.
distractorExplanations.d: Growth was present, so 'no growth' is inaccurate; mixed flora is reported with a specimen-quality comment.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-micro-058.explanation: Specimen quality. This item asks: “A plate with mixed skin flora on a poorly collected wound is:”. The matching answer is: Likely contamination — comment, do not over-work garbage. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official ASCP MLT paper. Do not overwork a poorly collected specimen.

options.a: Sniff plates to check for a characteristic odor
options.b: Open bench work with gloves and a surgical mask
options.c: Do not sniff plates; work in the right cabinet
options.d: Work in a laminar-flow clean bench

distractorExplanations.a: Sniffing plates risks aerosol exposure; Brucella is a leading cause of laboratory-acquired infection.
distractorExplanations.b: Brucella needs a biosafety cabinet with BSL-3 practices; a surgical mask does not protect against aerosols.
distractorExplanations.d: A clean bench protects the product, not the worker, and blows air toward the user; a Class II BSC is needed.

options.a: Perform and read Gram stains on clinical specimens
options.b: Call critical results to the licensed caregiver
options.c: Reject specimens that fail acceptance criteria
options.d: Choose the patient's antibiotic as the attending

distractorExplanations.a: Performing and reading Gram stains are core MLT tasks, so this is within the MLT's scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Calling criticals with read-back is an MLT responsibility, so this is within the MLT's scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Rejecting improperly collected specimens per SOP is part of the MLT role, so this is within scope.
